title_en: Guiding Case No. 221: Zhang v. Yibin HengMou Investment Group Co., Ltd., Sichuan Yibin WuMou Building Materials Industry Co., Ltd., et al. — monopoly dispute
ruling_gist_en: No person shall benefit from his or her illegal act. Horizontal monopoly agreements are obviously illegal. Where a business operator that participated in a horizontal monopoly agreement sues another operator that also participated in the same agreement, claiming compensation for losses incurred during the period of participation and performance of the agreement pursuant to the provisions on civil liability under the Anti-Monopoly Law of the People's Republic of China, the people's court shall not support such claim.

full_text_en:
Guiding Case No. 221

Zhang v. Yibin HengMou Investment Group Co., Ltd.,
Yibin WuMou Building Materials Industry Co., Ltd. (Sichuan Province), et al.
— monopoly dispute

(Adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on December 15, 2023)

Keywords
Civil; monopoly; horizontal monopoly agreement; implementer of monopolistic conduct; damages

Ruling Gist
No one shall benefit from his own illegal acts. A horizontal monopoly agreement is clearly an illegal act. If a business operator who participated in a horizontal monopoly agreement sues other participants in that agreement for compensation for losses incurred during its participation in and performance of the agreement, based on the provisions on civil liability under the Anti-Monopoly Law of the People's Republic of China, the people's court shall not support the claim.

Basic Facts
In March 2010, the Yibin City Civil Affairs Bureau of Sichuan Province approved the establishment of the Yibin City Mou Association (hereinafter referred to as the Mou Association), which was an industry-specific social organization. Cao served as its president, Ruan as its vice president, and Chen as its secretary-general. The founders and founding entities were Cao and Yibin City HengMou Group Co., Ltd., Li Gao and Yibin WuMou Building Materials Industry Co., Ltd. (Sichuan Province) (hereinafter referred to as WuMou Company), and Ruan and Yibin County SiMou Building Materials Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as SiMou Company). Initially, the Mou Association had more than 50 member units, including the Yibin City MouDian Machine-Made Brick Factory (hereinafter referred to as the MouDian Brick Factory) owned by Zhang.

In July 2009, the "Yibin City Brick Manufacturing Industry Working Meeting" was held. The Meeting Minutes recorded: the title was "Over-supply, low prices... balance of supply and demand, scarcity makes things precious..."; the specific plan was to establish a Brick Association Council and a Brick Association Coordination Office. The scope of activities included brick factories within 30 kilometers of Cuiping District of Yibin City and within 15 kilometers of Baixi. It was to coordinate with Yibin RenMou Trading Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as RenMou Company) in establishing local brick associations in surrounding counties and districts to prevent external products from entering the region. The shutdown plan proposed to shut down 50% of the brick factories, with operating brick factories subsidizing those shut down. RenMou Company, together with the Brick Association Coordination Office, would enter into lease and contract agreements with shut-down factories and cooperation agreements with operating factories. Shut-down factories would receive monthly lease and contract fees from RenMou Company (which were part of the management fees paid by the operating factories), and operating factories would pay market management and technical guidance fees to RenMou Company. In addition, it was provided that: "The shutdown and adjustment of brick factories must be determined by the Brick Association; no factory may adjust without authorization; any factory making an adjustment shall be deemed in breach, with a penalty of RMB 200,000 per breach, to be collected by the Coordination Office and RenMou Company." "Shut-down brick factories, after ceasing production, shall not sell their inventory bricks; there shall be a uniform cut-off without exception... private sales shall be deemed a breach, with the penalty being ten times the sales amount." Around the same time, the predecessor of the Mou Association, a certain branch association, formulated the "Interim Management Measures of a Branch of the Yibin Building Materials Industry Association" (hereinafter referred to as the "Interim Management Measures"), which explicitly set out specific arrangements to "prevent external products from entering and internally control brick and tile output," dividing local brick and tile enterprises into operating enterprises and shut-down enterprises. In July 2009, the branch association entered into agreements such as the "Shutdown and Rectification Contract" and the "Technical Service Contract" with brick and tile factories including the MouDian Brick Factory. According to the "Detailed List of Approved Output of Yibin City Brick Factories (Operating Factories)," there were 19 operating factories. According to the "Detailed List of Approved Output of Yibin City Brick Factories (Shut-down Factories)," there were 31 shut-down factories, including the MouDian Brick Factory.

On March 31, 2011, the Yibin City Economic and Information Technology Commission of Sichuan Province (hereinafter referred to as the Yibin City Economic and Information Technology Commission) issued the "Notice Ordering the Yibin City Mou Association to Suspend Activities," which stated: "We have recently received reports from the public that, during your activities, you have not strictly followed the association's章程 and have engaged in conduct beyond the scope stipulated in the association's章程. Pursuant to the requirements for the management of industry associations, you are hereby ordered to immediately and temporarily cease all activities of the association, conduct a comprehensive rectification, and report the rectification status to us in writing." On April 18, 2011, the Mou Association submitted to the Yibin City Economic and Information Technology Commission the "Report on the Rectification Work and Request to Resume Normal Activities of the Mou Association," which stated: "Because the association's principal leaders did not fully perform their duties... some individual brick factories artificially inflated prices and created false information of tight supply and demand... We believe that the brick association bears an undeniable responsibility for such outcomes and must correct them promptly..." "We have set clear goals: first, to unconditionally meet market demand... second, to supply goods at reasonable market prices (currently, the guidance price approved by the relevant authorities is: ex-factory price not exceeding RMB 0.33 per standard brick), and no member unit is allowed to supply goods at prices higher than the association's guidance price; third, to ensure quality..." In September 2011, the Mou Association stopped distributing shutdown support funds.

On March 6, 2013, the Sichuan Provincial Administration for Industry and Commerce issued an "Administrative Penalty Decision" against the Mou Association, finding that the "Interim Management Measures" reached by the Mou Association with its member units, which were in competition with each other, agreed that some enterprises would shut down, thereby controlling the production volume of bricks in the Yibin brick and tile market, controlling the withdrawal of shut-down member units from competition in the Yibin brick and tile market, and severely restricting market competition. This constituted a monopoly agreement restricting the quantity of commodity production. The conduct of the party in organizing member units to reach and implement the monopoly agreement disrupted the fair and orderly competitive order of the Yibin brick and tile market.

Subsequently, Zhang filed a lawsuit with the people's court, claiming that he ceased production pursuant to the "Shutdown and Rectification Contract" and received only a small amount of shutdown support funds before September 2011. The above conduct effectively excluded Zhang from participating in competition, constituted monopolistic conduct, and infringed his lawful rights and interests. He sought a judgment ordering WuMou Company, SiMou Company, Yibin HengMou Investment Group Co., Ltd., the Mou Association, Cao, and others to jointly and severally compensate him for economic losses of RMB 336,000 and reasonable expenses of RMB 80,000.

Judgment
The Chengdu Intermediate People's Court of Sichuan Province rendered a civil judgment on December 24, 2019 ((2018) Chuan 01 Min Chu No. 855): 1. Within fifteen days of the judgment taking effect, WuMou Company, SiMou Company, Cao, and the Mou Association shall jointly and severally compensate Zhang for economic losses of RMB 336,000 and reasonable expenses of RMB 5,000. 2. Zhang's other claims were dismissed. After the judgment was pronounced, WuMou Company, Cao, and the Mou Association appealed to the Supreme People's Court. The Supreme People's Court rendered a civil judgment on November 6, 2020 ((2020) Zui Gao Fa Zhi Min Zhong No. 1382): 1. The civil judgment of the Chengdu Intermediate People's Court of Sichuan Province ((2018) Chuan 01 Min Chu No. 855) was reversed. 2. All of Zhang's claims were dismissed.

Reasoning
The Supreme People's Court held: As Zhang was one of the implementers of the horizontal monopoly agreement in this case, whether he was entitled to claim from other implementers of the monopoly agreement compensation for his alleged economic losses should be considered in light of the legislative purpose of Article 50 of the Anti-Monopoly Law, the characteristics of the alleged monopolistic conduct, and the legal effects of damages, among other factors.

First, the legislative purpose of Article 50 of the Anti-Monopoly Law. Article 50 provides that where a business operator engages in monopolistic conduct and causes losses to others, it shall bear civil liability in accordance with the law. The legislative purpose of this article is to provide a civil judicial channel for stopping and combating monopolistic conduct and to provide civil remedies to persons harmed by such conduct. If the plaintiff is not a victim of the monopolistic conduct regulated by the Anti-Monopoly Law, but rather an implementer of that conduct, its claim for damages is essentially a demand for a share of the monopoly profits, and therefore it is not an object that the Anti-Monopoly Law intends to remedy. In this case, Zhang was a participant in and implementer of the horizontal monopoly agreement he alleged, and through participating in and implementing the alleged monopolistic conduct, he shared in the monopoly benefits for a certain period; he was not a victim of the monopolistic conduct intended to be remedied by the Anti-Monopoly Law.

Second, a party seeking damages must have lawful and proper conduct. A party that itself participates in and implements an illegal act, even if it suffers losses as a result, cannot obtain relief for those losses due to the illegality of its own conduct. Zhang voluntarily accepted the shutdown and rectification under the "Shutdown and Rectification Contract," participated in and implemented the horizontal monopoly agreement in this case, and his conduct was itself illegal; the losses he thereby suffered should not be remedied.

Finally, granting damages to implementers of monopolistic conduct would produce the negative legal effect of encouraging and supporting the relevant monopolistic conduct. In this case, the losses Zhang claimed to have suffered from the monopolistic conduct essentially amounted to a demand for enforcement of the horizontal monopoly agreement in this case and a division of the monopoly gains among the group in accordance with the agreement's allocation of monopoly profits. If Zhang's claim were upheld, it would in effect maintain and encourage the illegal conduct.

In conclusion, an implementer of a horizontal monopoly agreement is not entitled, under the Anti-Monopoly Law, to claim from other implementers of that agreement compensation for its alleged economic losses. As Zhang was an implementer of the horizontal monopoly agreement at issue, he is not entitled to benefit from his own illegal conduct, and the people's court does not support his claim for damages.

Related Legal Provisions
Article 60, Paragraph 1 of the Anti-Monopoly Law of the People's Republic of China (as amended in 2022) (the applicable provision in this case is Article 50 of the Anti-Monopoly Law of the People's Republic of China, as effective in 2008)
